titleEn: I will exalt you, my God the King
progression: | C G | Am Em | F C | G C |
intro: Twenty-one verses, one for each letter the psalm actually uses. It runs alef to tav in order and skips one letter: no verse begins with nun, so the mem verse at 13 is followed straight away by the samekh verse at 14. Said three times a day in the liturgy, where it is called Ashrei after the two verses fixed to its front and closed with a verse borrowed from Psalm 115. There is no enemy addressed here, no complaint and no request. The only people in it who come to harm appear in the last four words of verse 20.

stichs.en: A praise, of David.
I will exalt you, my God the King,
and bless your name for ever and ever.

verses.summary: This is the only psalm in the book whose heading calls it a praise, which is the word the whole collection is named after. The acrostic begins at the third word, and the first thing said is a title: my God the King.

stichs.en: Every day I will bless you,
and praise your name for ever and ever.

verses.summary: The commitment is made twice over, once as a daily habit and once as an endless span. The second half of the verse repeats the second half of verse 1 with a single word changed, bless becoming praise.

stichs.en: Great is the LORD and highly praised,
and his greatness cannot be fathomed.

verses.summary: Praise is stated and then declared impossible to finish, in the same breath. The remaining eighteen verses proceed anyway, which is the psalm's method rather than a contradiction in it.

stichs.en: One generation shall commend your works to the next,
and shall declare your mighty acts.

verses.summary: Praise is handed on rather than produced. From here to verse 12 nearly every verb is a speaking verb, and the speakers keep changing between the one voice and everybody.

stichs.en: The splendour of the glory of your majesty,
and the accounts of your wonders, I will speak.

verses.summary: Three nouns stacked in construct, each depending on the next, with one first person verb at the end carrying the whole pile.

stichs.en: And they shall tell the force of your awesome acts,
and I will recount your greatness.

verses.summary: They speak, then I speak. The psalm keeps alternating between the crowd and the single voice without ever choosing which one is doing the praising.

stichs.en: They shall pour out the memory of your great goodness,
and sing aloud of your righteousness.

verses.summary: Memory here carries the sense of reputation, what gets said about someone when he is not in the room. The verb for pouring out is used of water and of speech that cannot be held back.

stichs.en: The LORD is gracious and compassionate,
slow to anger and great in kindness.

verses.summary: The formula from Exodus 34, quoted in the shortened form that recurs across the prophets and the psalms. Here it is given as the ground of the praise rather than, as usually happens, as a plea for mercy.

stichs.en: The LORD is good to all,
and his mercies are over all his works.

verses.summary: The word all enters here and does not leave the psalm again. From this verse the subject is the reach of the care rather than its intensity.

stichs.en: All your works shall thank you, LORD,
and your faithful ones shall bless you.

verses.summary: Two choirs are set side by side, everything that was made and the people who keep faith, and they are given parallel verbs. Nothing in the line ranks one above the other.

stichs.en: They shall tell the glory of your kingdom,
and speak of your might.

verses.summary: Kingdom appears as a noun for the first time and the vocabulary turns political. Glory, might, dominion: this is the language of a royal court, applied to the God addressed as King in verse 1.

stichs.en: To make his mighty acts known to humankind,
and the glorious splendour of his kingdom.

verses.summary: The purpose clause the last eight verses were waiting for. All that telling has an audience, and the audience is not God: it is people who would otherwise not know.

stichs.en: Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages,
and your dominion in every generation.

verses.summary: The kingship claim at full extent, measured in time rather than in territory. Some manuscripts and ancient versions carry an extra line at this point, beginning with the letter the psalm otherwise skips.

stichs.en: The LORD upholds all who fall,
and straightens all who are bent down.

verses.summary: The first verse in which God does something for people in trouble. Both verbs are participles, so the holding up and the straightening are ongoing rather than finished events.

stichs.en: The eyes of all look to you in hope,
and you give them their food in its time.

verses.summary: Every creature is facing the same direction and waiting. The rare verb in the fourth word is the one used for watching out for something you expect to arrive.

stichs.en: You open your hand,
and satisfy every living thing with favour.

verses.summary: The verse the liturgy singles out of the whole psalm. A hand opens and everything alive is filled, and the last word is not food but favour, so what arrives is more than what was needed.

stichs.en: The LORD is righteous in all his ways,
and faithful in all his works.

verses.summary: Two words used throughout the psalms to describe good people are turned around and used of God, and each is qualified by in all, which is the harder claim of the two.

stichs.en: The LORD is near to all who call him,
to all who call him in truth.

verses.summary: The one place the psalm narrows. The first half says all who call, the second half repeats it and adds a condition, and the condition is about the caller rather than about what is asked for.

stichs.en: He does the desire of those who fear him,
and he hears their cry and saves them.

verses.summary: Three verbs in a row, and the order is strange: the desire is done, and only afterwards the cry is heard. The word for desire is the same word translated favour at the end of verse 16.

stichs.en: The LORD keeps all who love him,
but all the wicked he will destroy.

verses.summary: The single hard clause in the psalm, placed one verse from the end. Both halves are built the same way, so keeping and destroying are set out in one line as two applications of the same attention.

stichs.en: My mouth shall speak the praise of the LORD,
and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.

verses.summary: The mouth of verse 1 returns and then opens outward: my mouth, then all flesh. The final two words are the ones that ended verses 1 and 2, so the psalm closes on the phrase it began with.

pardes.body: An alphabet used as an argument. Each verse takes the next letter and adds one item to a single claim: this King is great, and his greatness is exercised as care. The first half is about speech, who does it and to whom, and the hinge is verse 12, which finally states that the point of all the telling is that people should know. From verse 14 the psalm stops describing praise and starts describing what is being praised: the fallen held up, everything alive fed, nearness to whoever calls. The sequence is not complete. Twenty-one verses carry twenty-one letters, alef through tav in order, and no verse begins with nun; the mem verse at {{13.0}} is followed immediately by the samekh verse at {{14.0}}.

The gap falls between {{13.0}} and {{14.0}}. A copy of this psalm found at Qumran carries a line in exactly that position beginning with the missing letter, and the Greek and Syriac versions carry a matching line, usually rendered as God is faithful in his words and gracious in all his deeds. Whether that line fell out of the text the Masoretes preserved or was supplied later by someone completing the alphabet is disputed, and the manuscripts on their own do not settle it. One detail worth weighing either way: the supplied line closes with the same three words that close the tsadi verse here, {{17.4}} to {{17.6}}. On a smaller scale, {{8.3}} and {{8.4}} read literally as long of nostrils, the Hebrew idiom for a slow temper, which is why the phrase cannot be put into English without losing the face it is describing.

The Talmud in tractate Berakhot asks straight out why this psalm has no nun verse, and answers that the letter would have started the word for falling, which is not something an alphabet of praise was going to carry. The same passage then points at the verse that does follow, {{14.0}}, which opens with the samekh of upholding: the fall is left unwritten and the holding up is written in its place. That passage is also where the practice of saying this psalm three times a day is grounded, and it singles out one verse as the reason, {{16.0}} to {{16.2}}, you open your hand. The codes take that seriously enough to rule that a person who says the psalm without attending to that verse says it again.

Read as a ladder, the psalm climbs from one mouth to all flesh, and the rungs are the letters. Kabbalistic reading treats the alphabet as the set of instruments the world was made with, so an alphabetical psalm is the whole toolkit turned back toward its owner. That makes the absent letter the point rather than a defect: the one thing the instruments are not used to spell is the fall, and the psalm passes it in silence and goes straight to the verse about holding people up. The open hand is read in the same key, as the standard image for an outflow that is not measured against the worth of what receives it, which is why the verse can say every living thing and leave it unqualified.
